summary.text: A terminating Sears transformation, derived from Pfaff–Saalschütz summations, rewrites the expression as \((3n+1)a(n)=(n+1)\sum_{2j\le n+1}\binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}\binom{n+j}{j}\binom{2n-j}{n}^2\). In the required range the squared last binomial contributes \(p^2\), and a case split supplies another \(p\) from \(n+1\), \(\binom{n+j}{j}\), or \(\binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}\); since \(2p<3n+1<3p\), the factor \(3n+1\) is coprime to \(p\) and can be cancelled.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}\binom{3n+2k}{n}.
\]
We prove that, if \(p\geq 5\) is prime and
\[
 \left\lceil\frac{2p+1}{3}\right\rceil\leq n\leq p-1,
\]
then \(p^3\mid a(n)\).

We begin with the hypergeometric identity that will put the summands into a form suitable for the divisibility argument.

## 1. A terminating hypergeometric transformation

For a rational number \(x\) and a nonnegative integer \(r\), write
\[
 (x)_r=x(x+1)\cdots(x+r-1),\qquad (x)_0=1
\]
for the rising factorial. We shall use the terminating Pfaff–Saalschütz evaluation
\[
\sum_{r=0}^{N}
 \frac{(-N)_r(a)_r(b)_r}
 {(c)_r(1+a+b-c-N)_r\,r!}
=
\frac{(c-a)_N(c-b)_N}{(c)_N(c-a-b)_N},                 \tag{1}
\]
whenever the displayed denominators are nonzero.

For completeness, here is a proof of (1). Denote the summand on the left by \(F_N(r)\), and put
\[
 \rho_N=\frac{(c-a+N)(c-b+N)}{(c+N)(c-a-b+N)}.
\]
The quotient of the proposed right-hand side at \(N+1\) by that at \(N\) is exactly \(\rho_N\). Thus it is enough to show that the sum on the left satisfies the same first-order recurrence.

Define
\[
 R_N(r)=
 \frac{r(c+r-1)(a+b-c+r-N)}
 {(c+N)(r-N-1)(a+b-c-N)}
\]
and \(G_N(r)=R_N(r)F_N(r)\). The elementary ratios
\[
\frac{F_N(r+1)}{F_N(r)}
=
\frac{(-N+r)(a+r)(b+r)}
 {(c+r)(1+a+b-c-N+r)(r+1)}

a
\]
and
\[
\frac{F_{N+1}(r)}{F_N(r)}
=
\frac{(-N-1)(a+b-c+r-N)}
 {(r-N-1)(a+b-c-N)}
\]
show, after putting both sides over a common denominator, that for the interior indices
\[
 F_{N+1}(r)-\rho_NF_N(r)=G_N(r+1)-G_N(r).             \tag{2}
\]
(The isolated letter “a” after the first displayed ratio is to be ignored; the ratio itself is the asserted formula.) Explicitly, after cancellation, (2) is the rational identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{(-N-1)(a+b-c+r-N)}{(r-N-1)(a+b-c-N)}-\rho_N\\
&\quad=R_N(r+1)
 \frac{(-N+r)(a+r)(b+r)}
 {(c+r)(1+a+b-c-N+r)(r+1)}-R_N(r),
\end{aligned}
\]
which follows by expansion of the two numerators. Also \(G_N(0)=0\). At the upper boundary, the two terms of the \((N+1)\)-sum not covered by the interior telescoping satisfy
\[
F_{N+1}(N)-\rho_NF_N(N)+F_{N+1}(N+1)+G_N(N)=0;
\]
this follows by inserting \(r=N\) in the displayed formulas and clearing the nonzero denominators. Summing (2), together with this boundary identity, gives
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{N+1}F_{N+1}(r)
 =\rho_N\sum_{r=0}^{N}F_N(r).
\]
Both sides of (1) are \(1\) when \(N=0\), and the proposed right-hand side has the same multiplier \(\rho_N\). Induction proves (1).

We now specialize (1) twice to prove the transformation needed here. Set
\[
 B=\frac{3n+1}{2},\qquad C=\frac{3n+2}{2},\qquad D=\frac{2n+1}{2}.
\]
Define
\[
 L_j= rac{(-n)_j^2(B)_j(C)_j}{(1)_j^2(D)_j\,j!}

a
\]
and
\[
 U_s= rac{(-n)_s^2(-n/2)_s(-(n+1)/2)_s}
 {(-2n)_s^2(D)_s\,s!}.
\]
We claim that
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^n L_j=\binom{2n}{n}^2\sum_{s=0}^n U_s.    \tag{3}
\]
Again, the stray isolated letter following the definition of \(L_j\) has no mathematical role; the definition is the displayed fraction.

Here is a derivation of (3). For \(0\leq j\leq n\), put
\[
 q_j= rac{(-n)_j^2(B)_j(C)_j}
 {(D)_j(-2n)_j^2j!},
\]
and, for \(0\leq \ell\leq n-j\), put
\[
 h_{j,\ell}=
 \frac{(-(n-j))_\ell(-n+j)_\ell(-2n-1)_\ell}
 {(-2n+j)_\ell^2\ell!}.
\]
Consider the finite triangular double sum over \(j,\ell\geq0\), \(j+\ell\leq n\).

First fix \(s=j+\ell\). Using
\[
 (x)_{r+t}=(x)_r(x+r)_t

a
\]
and the complementary-factor identity
\[
 \frac{(a)_{s-j}}{(s-j)!}
 =\frac{(a)_s}{s!}\frac{(-s)_j}{(1-a-s)_j},           \tag{4}
\]
we obtain
\[
 q_jh_{j,s-j}
 =A_s\,
 \frac{(-s)_j(B)_j(C)_j}
 {(D)_j(1+B+C-D-s)_j\,j!},                            \tag{5}
\]
where
\[
 A_s=\frac{(-n)_s^2}{(-2n)_s^2}\frac{(-2n-1)_s}{s!}.
\]
Identity (4) follows directly by writing out both products in reverse order. Summing (5) over \(0\leq j\leq s\), and applying (1) with \(N=s,a=B,b=C,c=D\), gives
\[
\sum_{j=0}^s q_jh_{j,s-j}
=A_s\frac{(D-B)_s(D-C)_s}{(D)_s(D-B-C)_s}.
\]
Now
\[
 D-B=-\frac n2,
 \qquad D-C=-\frac{n+1}{2},
 \qquad D-B-C=-(2n+1).
\]
Thus the factor \((-2n-1)_s\) in \(A_s\) cancels the last denominator, and consequently
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^s q_jh_{j,s-j}=U_s.                       \tag{6}
\]
All canceled rising factorials are nonzero because \(s\leq n<2n+1\); the case \(n=s=0\) is immediate.

Second, fix \(j\). Apply (1) with
\[
 N=n-j,\qquad a=-n+j,
 \qquad b=-2n-1,
 \qquad c=-2n+j.
\]
The second lower parameter is again \(-2n+j\), so this gives
\[
\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-j}h_{j,\ell}
=
\frac{(-n)_{n-j}(j+1)_{n-j}}
 {(-2n+j)_{n-j}(n+1)_{n-j}}.                          \tag{7}
\]
No denominator vanishes in the indicated range: a negative integral rising factorial \((-M)_r\) is nonzero for \(r\leq M\), while every positive rising factorial is nonzero.

A direct factorial simplification of (7) yields
\[
 \binom{2n}{n}^2q_j
 \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-j}h_{j,\ell}=L_j.                  \tag{8}
\]
For clarity, this simplification uses only
\[
 (-M)_r=(-1)^r\frac{M!}{(M-r)!},
 \qquad (m+1)_r=\frac{(m+r)!}{m!}.
\]
Indeed these formulas show that
\[
\binom{2n}{n}^2
\frac{(-n)_{n-j}(j+1)_{n-j}}
 {(-2n+j)_{n-j}(n+1)_{n-j}}
= rac{(-2n)_j^2}{(1)_j^2},
\]
which, multiplied by \(q_j\), is exactly \(L_j\).

Finally, reindexing the finite triangle gives
\[
 \sum_{s=0}^n\sum_{j=0}^sq_jh_{j,s-j}
 =\sum_{j=0}^n\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-j}q_jh_{j,\ell}.
\]
Using (6) on the left and (8) on the right proves (3).

## 2. Conversion of (3) to binomial coefficients

We use the elementary formulas
\[
 \frac{(-m)_r}{r!}=(-1)^r\binom mr\quad(0\leq r\leq m),                 \tag{9}
\]
\[
 (x)_{2r}=4^r(x/2)_r((x+1)/2)_r,                                      \tag{10}
\]
and
\[
 \frac{(m+1)_r}{r!}=\binom{m+r}{r}.                                   \tag{11}
\]
Writing out factorials and using (9)–(11), the left summand in (3) becomes
\[
 L_k
 =\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}
   \frac{\binom{3n+2k}{n}}{\binom{3n}{n}}.                            \tag{12}
\]
For example, (10) combines the factors \(((3n+1)/2)_k((3n+2)/2)_k\), and comparison of the resulting consecutive products gives the last two binomial factors in (12).

Likewise, the transformed summand is
\[
 U_j=
 \frac{\binom nj^2\binom{n+1}{2j}\binom{n+j}{j}}
 {\binom{2n}{j}^2\binom{2n+2j}{2j}}.                                 \tag{13}
\]
If \(2j\leq n+1\), this follows from (9)–(11) and (10), now applied to the pair \((-n/2)_j(-(n+1)/2)_j\). If \(2j>n+1\), that pair has product zero: by (10) it is a nonzero scalar multiple of \((-(n+1))_{2j}\), which contains a zero factor. The right side of (13) is also zero because \(\binom{n+1}{2j}=0\). Thus (13) is valid for every \(0\leq j\leq n\).

Multiplying (3) by \(\binom{3n}{n}\) and using (12) and (13), we obtain the rational identity
\[
 a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}\binom{2n}{n}^2
 \sum_{j=0}^n
 \frac{\binom nj^2\binom{n+1}{2j}\binom{n+j}{j}}
 {\binom{2n}{j}^2\binom{2n+2j}{2j}}.                                 \tag{14}
\]

We next turn (14) into an identity entirely in integers. For \(2j\leq n+1\), direct cancellation of factorials gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\binom{3n}{n}\binom{2n}{n}^2
 \frac{\binom nj^2\binom{n+1}{2j}\binom{n+j}{j}}
 {\binom{2n}{j}^2\binom{2n+2j}{2j}}\\
&\qquad=
 \frac{n+1}{3n+1}
 \binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}\binom{n+j}{j}
 \binom{2n-j}{n}^2.                                                    \tag{15}
\end{aligned}
\]
To see this, replace every binomial coefficient by its factorial expression. The complementary factorial in the first binomial on the right is
\[
(3n+1)-(n+1-2j)=2n+2j,
\]
and the complementary factorial in the last one is
\[
(2n-j)-n=n-j.
\]
After these substitutions all factorials cancel, with the only remaining scalar factor being \((n+1)/(3n+1)\). If \(2j>n+1\), the corresponding term in (14) is zero. Summing (15) therefore gives the integer identity
\[
(3n+1)a(n)=(n+1)\sum_{\substack{0\leq j\leq n\\2j\leq n+1}}
 \binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}\binom{n+j}{j}\binom{2n-j}{n}^2.                 \tag{16}
\]
This is the key transformation.

## 3. The divisibility of every transformed summand

Assume henceforth that \(p\geq5\) is prime and
\[
\left\lceil\frac{2p+1}{3}\right\rceil\leq n\leq p-1.                \tag{17}
\]
For integral division,
\[
\left\lceil\frac{2p+1}{3}\right\rceil
=\left\lfloor\frac{2p+3}{3}\right\rfloor.
\]
Because \(p\geq5\) is prime, \(p\not\equiv0\pmod3\). If \(p=3q+1\), the lower bound is \(2q+1\); if \(p=3q+2\), it is \(2q+2\). In either case (17) implies
\[
 3n+1>2p.                                                             \tag{18}
\]
It also implies \(n<p\).

We repeatedly use the following elementary consequence of Legendre's formula, equivalently the one-carry case of Kummer's theorem. If \(0\leq r,s<p\) and \(r+s\geq p\), then
\[
 p\mid\binom{r+s}{r}.                                                 \tag{19}
\]
Indeed, \((r+s)!\) contains one factor \(p\), whereas neither \(r!\) nor \(s!\) contains one. We shall also use the general carry formulation: the exponent of \(p\) in \(\binom XY\) is the number of carries when \(Y\) and \(X-Y\) are added in base \(p\). This follows immediately from
\[
 v_p(M!)=\sum_{e\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{M}{p^e}\right\rfloor.
\]

Fix \(j\) with \(2j\leq n+1\). We first prove
\[
 p\mid\binom{2n-j}{n}.                                                \tag{20}
\]
The two lower parts of this binomial coefficient are \(n\) and \(n-j\), both less than \(p\). Moreover,
\[
 2n-j\geq p.
\]
Indeed, \(j\leq(n+1)/2\), so
\[
2n-j\geq\frac{3n-1}{2}\geq p,
\]
where the last inequality follows from the two residue-class forms of the lower bound just noted. Thus \(n+(n-j)\geq p\), and (19) proves (20). Consequently the square \(\binom{2n-j}{n}^2\) supplies two factors of \(p\).

It remains to find one more factor of \(p\) in
\[
 (n+1)\binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}\binom{n+j}{j}.                             \tag{21}
\]
There are three cases.

### Case 1: \(p\mid n+1\)

Then the required factor is already present in \(n+1\).

### Case 2: \(p\nmid n+1\) and \(n+j\geq p\)

Since \(n+1\leq p\) and \(p\nmid n+1\), we have \(n+1<p\), hence \(n<p\). Also \(j<p\). The two lower parts of \(\binom{n+j}{j}\) are \(j\) and \(n\), both below \(p\), while their sum is at least \(p\). Therefore (19) gives
\[
 p\mid\binom{n+j}{j}.
\]

### Case 3: \(p\nmid n+1\) and \(n+j<p\)

Again \(n+1<p\). Put
\[
 m=n+1-2j,
 \qquad N=3n+1.
\]
Then \(0\leq m<p\), and
\[
 N-m=2n+2j.
\]
By (18), \(2n+2j\geq p\). On the other hand, \(n+j<p\), so
\[
 2n+2j<2p.
\]
Thus the units digit modulo \(p\) of \(N-m\) is \(2n+2j-p\), while the units digit of \(m\) is \(m\). Their sum is
\[
 m+(2n+2j-p)=3n+1-p>p

a
\]
by (18). Hence adding \(m\) and \(N-m\) in base \(p\) produces a carry in the units place.

There can be no issue from higher powers obscuring this argument: from \(n\leq p-1\),
\[
 N=3n+1\leq3p-2<p^2
\]
for \(p\geq5\). Kummer's carry criterion therefore gives
\[
 p\mid\binom{3n+1}{m}
 =\binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}.
\]

Thus in every case,
\[
 p\mid (n+1)\binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}\binom{n+j}{j}.                       \tag{22}
\]
Combining (20), squared, with (22), we conclude that for every surviving index \(j\),
\[
 p^3\mid
 (n+1)\binom{3n+1}{n+1-2j}\binom{n+j}{j}\binom{2n-j}{n}^2.          \tag{23}
\]
Every omitted index \(2j>n+1\) contributes zero, which is of course also divisible by \(p^3\). Therefore the whole right-hand side of (16) is divisible by \(p^3\), and (16) yields
\[
 p^3\mid (3n+1)a(n).                                                   \tag{24}
\]

## 4. Cancellation of the prefactor

It remains only to show that \(p\nmid3n+1\). From (18),
\[
 2p<3n+1.
\]
Since \(n\leq p-1\),
\[
 3n+1\leq3p-2<3p.
\]
Thus \(3n+1\) lies strictly between \(2p\) and \(3p\), an interval containing no multiple of \(p\). Hence
\[
 \gcd(p^3,3n+1)=1.
\]
Euclid's lemma applied to (24) now allows us to cancel \(3n+1\), giving
\[
 p^3\mid a(n).
\]
This holds for every prime \(p\geq5\) and every integer \(n\) in the stated interval, as required.
